items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the following inequality:

Content:
[MATH: x > 0]

Content:
We can represent this inequality using a number line as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/54ef88735840139200de941c31faa476]

Content:
How do we represent this inequality using interval notation?

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- The left endpoint [MATH: x=0] is not included. Therefore, we use a parenthesis [MATH: (] for this endpoint.
- The interval continues forever in the positive direction. To denote this, we must introduce the infinity symbol [MATH: \infty.] Infinity is not a number but a concept that means larger than any number.
- We use a right parenthesis [MATH: )] in conjunction with the [MATH: \infty] symbol.

Content:
Therefore, we can express the inequality [MATH: x > 0] in interval notation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x \in (0, \infty)]

Content:
Watch Out! Whenever [MATH: \infty] appears in an interval, it is always associated with a right parenthesis. Infinity is never associated with a bracket, even if the other endpoint is.

items.title: Converting Inequalities to Left-Bounded Intervals

sections.normalized_html: Express the inequality [MATH: x \geq 1] in interval notation.
sections.readable_text: Express the inequality [MATH: x \geq 1] in interval notation.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The inequality [MATH: x \geq 1] corresponds to all numbers greater than or equal to [MATH: 1.] A number line for this inequality is shown below:

From the segment on the number line, we have the following:

  • The left endpoint [MATH: 1] is included in the interval.

  • There is no right endpoint - it continues forever. So, we write the interval with infinity as the right endpoint, not included.

Therefore, using interval notation, we represent [MATH: x \geq 1] as

[MATH: x \in [1,\infty).]

items.title: Converting Left-Bounded Intervals to Inequalities

sections.normalized_html: What inequality corresponds the interval [MATH: x\in\left[5, \infty\right)?]
sections.readable_text: What inequality corresponds the interval [MATH: x\in\left[5, \infty\right)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The statement [MATH: x\in\left[5, \infty\right)] means that [MATH: x] lies between [MATH: 5] and [MATH: \infty,] where

  • the left endpoint [MATH: 5] is included, and

  • the right endpoint [MATH: \infty] is not included.

Therefore, the inequality represented by this interval is

[MATH: 5 \leq x < \infty.]

However, since all numbers are smaller than infinity, it suffices to write

[MATH: 5 \leq x] or, equivalently, [MATH: x \geq 5.]
